newsitem.title: USA: Hispanics to stage first major march in Washington.
newsitem.headline: Hispanics to stage first major march in Washington.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Hispanics are to stage on Saturday their first major march in the United States' capital, organisers said on Friday.

The Latino March, which will end with a rally on the Ellipse behind the White House, was summoned to protest against recent welfare and immigration reform legislation, which Hispanic advocates view as part of a rising tide of discrimination.

The organisers, mostly young grassroots and labour activists with a more radical agenda than the older Latino leadership, also hope to stake out a larger political role for their community at a national level.

"This is the only way in which we are going to gain ... the quota of power we deserve, both politically and economically," said Los Angeles-based lawyer Juan Jose Gutierrez, 39, one of the leaders of the Coordinadora '96 march organising team.
"So far all we have received is scorn, even though almost all of our men and women work, sometimes holding down two jobs, and pay taxes," he added.
Coordinadora '96 drew up a seven-point political platform that has caused some of the more traditional Latino advocacy groups to balk at endorsing the march.

Among the planks are calls for an increase in the minimum wage to $7 an hour, free education from kindergarten through university, and an amnesty for illegal immigrants who entered the United States before 1992.
Besides a long list of speakers, the rally will feature artists such as salsa singer Willie Colon and several bands to highlight the Latino community's contribution to U.S. cultural life.

Young Latino activists hold that, even though Hispanics are bound to overtake blacks early next century as the largest racial minority in the United States, they are still politically under-represented and poorly organised.

Saturday's march would be their largest demonstration since some 250,000 people took to the streets of Los Angeles in October 1994 to protest against California's Proposition 187, a ballot initiative designed to deny free state services to illegal immigrants and their children.

Since then, and in response to similar proposals put forward by Republicans in Congress, Gutierrez and other activists like him in major cities have led a drive to persuade foreign-born Hispanics to become U.S. citizens and register to vote.
The Immigration and Naturalisation Service estimates that a record 1.1 million people were sworn in as American citizens over the past 12 months, more than double the number of the previous year.
